If you’re thinking about filing for divorce, one of the first questions you may have is whether you need a specific reason—or “grounds”—to legally end your marriage. Many people assume they must prove fault, such as infidelity or misconduct, but that is not how divorce works in Colorado.

Colorado divorce laws take a different approach, focusing less on blame and more on resolution. Understanding the legal grounds for divorce in Colorado can help you move forward with clarity and confidence.

Let’s break it down.

Is Colorado a No-Fault Divorce State?

Yes. Colorado is a no-fault divorce state, which means that neither spouse is required to prove wrongdoing to obtain a divorce.

Instead of assigning blame, Colorado courts only require one legal ground for divorce:

The irretrievable breakdown of the marriage.

This approach is designed to reduce conflict and allow couples to focus on resolving practical matters such as parenting time, property division, and financial support.

What Does “Irretrievable Breakdown” Mean?

“Irretrievable breakdown” is a legal term used to describe a marriage that cannot be repaired. In practical terms, it means that the relationship has broken down to the point where reconciliation is not realistic.

Examples of situations that may lead to an irretrievable breakdown include:

  • Ongoing conflict or lack of communication
  • Emotional or physical separation
  • Loss of trust or connection
  • Fundamental differences that cannot be resolved

Importantly, you do not need to prove these issues in court. A statement that the marriage is irretrievably broken is generally sufficient.

Do Both Spouses Have to Agree?

No. Colorado does not require both spouses to agree that the marriage is over.

  • If one spouse believes the marriage is irretrievably broken, the court can proceed with the divorce.
  • If the other spouse disagrees, the court may allow time for counseling or reconciliation efforts, but it is not required to deny the divorce.

Ultimately, Colorado law recognizes that a marriage cannot be forced to continue if one party no longer wishes to remain married.

Are Fault-Based Reasons Ever Considered?

While fault is not required to obtain a divorce, certain behaviors may still be relevant to other aspects of the case.

For example:

  • Domestic violence may affect child custody and parenting time decisions.
  • Financial misconduct, such as hiding assets, can impact property division.
  • Substance abuse may be considered when determining the best interests of a child.

These issues do not serve as grounds for divorce, but they can influence how the court resolves related matters.

Why Colorado Uses a No-Fault Divorce System

Colorado’s no-fault approach is intended to:

  • Reduce unnecessary conflict and litigation
  • Encourage cooperation and settlement
  • Focus court involvement on protecting children and ensuring fairness

By removing the need to prove fault, the process often becomes more efficient and less emotionally taxing for families.

Common Misconceptions About Divorce Grounds in Colorado

Some common myths include:

  • “I can’t file unless my spouse cheated.”
    ❌ Not true. Cheating is not required to file.
  • “I have to prove my spouse did something wrong.”
    ❌ Colorado law does not require proof of misconduct.
  • “If my spouse disagrees, I can’t get divorced.”
    ❌ One spouse’s belief that the marriage is over is enough.

Understanding these misconceptions can help you approach the process with realistic expectations.
